title: On additive differential probabilities of the composition of bitwise exclusive-or and a bit rotation
authors: Nikolay Kolomeec, Ivan Sutormin, Denis Bykov, Matvey Panferov, Tatyana Bonich
text:
ARX is one of the modern architectures for symmetric cryptography primitives that uses only three operations: addition modulo 2^{n} (Addition, \boxplus), circular shift (Rotation, \lll) and bitwise addition modulo 2 (XOR, \oplus). Examples of such schemes include block ciphers FEAL [1], Speck [2], stream ciphers Salsa20 [3] and ChaCha [4], SHA-3 finalists BLAKE [5] and Skein [6], MAC algorithm Chaskey [7]. ARX constructions have many advantages: fast performance and compactness of its program implementation, resistance to timing attacks. However, it is difficult to determine if they are secure against differential cryptanalysis [8]. This method requires studying how input differences transform to the output differences.

In this work we consider differences that are expressed using addition modulo 2^{n}. In some cases they are more appropriate than XOR differences, especially if round keys are added modulo 2^{n} and the number of XOR operations is much less than the number of modulo 2^{n} operations, see, for instance, [9]. Some information related to differential cryptanalysis of ARX constructions and choosing differences can be found in [10,11]. The additive differential probability \mathrm{adp}^{f}(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\to\alpha_{k+1}) for a function f:(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n})^{k}\to\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}, where \alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k+1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}, is defined as

Here \alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k} and \alpha_{k+1} are its input differences and its output difference respectively, x_{1},\ldots,x_{k} are uniformly distributed. The additive differential probability of a rotation (\mathrm{adp}^{\lll}) and XOR (\mathrm{adp}^{\oplus}) were studied in [12,13] and [14,15,16]. The formula for the additive differential probability \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{RX}} for the composition (x\lll r)\oplus y was obtained in [17]. Also, it was pointed out that it is inaccurate to calculate differential probability of the composition by assuming that the inputs of the basic operations are independent (the same is true for XOR differences, see, for instance, [18]). Note that we can add \boxplus operation to a composition and express new differential probabilities from the old ones in a direct way, since the considered differences go through \boxplus with probability one. For instance, it works for the function ((x\boxplus z)\lll r)\oplus y if we know differential probabilities for (x\lll r)\oplus y.

We investigate the properties of \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}} for the function (x\oplus y)\lll r, where x,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n} and 1\leq r\leq n-1. They are similar to the properties of \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{RX}} since \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}}(\alpha,\beta\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\to}}\gamma)=\mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{RX}}(\gamma,\beta\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n-r}}{{\to}}\alpha). Though there is the formula for \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{RX}}, many its properties are still unknown. First of all, we study maximums of \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}}, where the rotation is one bit left/right and one of the first two arguments is fixed. More precisely, we find \beta^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime} such that \max_{\beta,\gamma}\mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}}(\alpha,\beta\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\to}}\gamma)=\mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}}(\alpha,\beta^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\to}}\gamma^{\prime}), where r=1 (one bit left rotation) and r=n-1 (one bit right rotation). One bit rotations are used, for instance, in CHAM [19,20] (see also COMET [21] which is based on CHAM and Speck) and Alzette [22] (see also Sparkle [23]). Note that we do not analyze maximums for other argument fixations as well as for other rotations. These cases look more difficult. In addition, we obtain some symmetries of \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}}. They allow us to construct distinct differentials whose probabilities are the same. Finally, we provide all impossible differentials (i.e. differentials with probability zero) of the function (x\oplus y)\lll r in terms of regular expression patterns. The lower and upper bounds for the numbers of them are \frac{1}{8}8^{n} and \frac{5}{14}8^{n} respectively. Similar number for the function x\oplus y obtained in [14] is \lfloor\frac{4}{7}8^{n}\rfloor. We can say that the rotation significantly reduces the number of impossible differentials. Overall, the maximums \max_{\beta,\gamma}\mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}}(\alpha,\beta\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\to}}\gamma) for r=1 and r=n-1 are very similar to maximums of \mathrm{adp}^{\oplus}. More precisely, they coincide for the one bit left rotation (Corollary 3) and coincide at least half the time for the one bit right rotation (Corollary 4). Also, the number of impossible differentials is maximal for the one bit left rotation. It may be an additional reason to consider these rotations as the simplest ones. ‘‘Maximal’’ differentials are used to construct differential trails, whereas impossible differentials are of interest because of impossible differential cryptanalysis [24,25]. There are techniques for finding them for a wide class of transformations, see, for instance, [26,27]. Some attacks (and approaches) against ARX ciphers can be found in [28,29,30].

The paper is organized as follows. Necessary definitions are given in Section 2. In Section 3, we introduce auxiliary notions (\mathrm{adp}^{\oplus}_{c} and \mathrm{adp}^{\oplus}_{a,b}) and rewrite the formula from [17] to obtain an expression for \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}} in these terms (Theorem 2 and Corollary 2). Section 4 is devoted to the argument symmetries of \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}} which turn out to be similar to the symmetries of \mathrm{adp}^{\oplus} (Theorem 5). Section 5 describes maximums of \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}}, where the rotation is one bit left/right and one of the first two arguments is fixed (Theorem 6 in Section 5.1 for the one bit left rotation and Theorem 7 in Section 5.2 for the one bit right rotation). Section 6 provides all impossible differentials of the XR-operation (Theorem 9 and Table 4 in Section 6.2) in terms of regular expression patterns (see Section 6.1). Some auxiliary results are moved to Appendix A. Also, several estimations of the number \mathcal{N}_{n}^{r} of tuples (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n} such that \mathrm{adp}^{\mathrm{XR}}(\alpha,\beta\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\to}}\gamma)=0 are given in Section 6.3 (Corollaries 5 and 6). The most significant of them are \frac{1}{8}8^{n}\leq\frac{1}{7}8^{n}-\frac{1}{7}8^{r}\leq\mathcal{N}_{n}^{r}<\lfloor\frac{5}{14}8^{n}\rfloor=\mathcal{N}_{n}^{1}, where 2\leq r<n.
